content:
Hi everyone,

We are releasing Archon Horizon, an open-source, workspace-first orchestration system for long-running Lean 4 formalization with Codex or Claude Code.

Some of you are already using Archon. Horizon is not intended to replace it, but to provide an alternative for more ambitious projects and more capable long-running models. Archon focuses on formalization with models such as Sonnet, Opus, or DeepSeek within a single run and project. Horizon is particularly suited to models such as Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol working across many sessions and interdependent projects. Furthermore, because these advanced models are already highly autonomous, rigid pipelines and detailed instructions can actually hinder them, therefore Horizon maintains a flexible, unconstrained workflow.

Archon follows a fairly deterministic loop: plan -> prove -> review. This helps control context size and keeps planning explicit. Horizon instead follows a deliberately simpler loop: horizon -> horizon -> horizon -> .... Each iteration is a fresh agent session operating on the same durable workspace.

In practice, the pipeline works as follows:

  1. A human or supervising AI creates a task, or asks Horizon to select work from the current project state.
  2. A Horizon session reconstructs the relevant context from the task, roadmap, blueprint, dependency graph, inbox, and richly annotated Git history.
  3. The session works autonomously using the available tools, including the Lean LSP server, local and semantic search, Git, inboxes, and native subagents.
  4. While it works, Horizon surfaces messages, related sessions, protected files, and potentially overlapping scopes so that parallel teams can coordinate.
  5. During the sessions, the agent commits its changes. At the end of the session, and writes a report recording its progress, remaining problems, and suggested next steps.
  6. A later session continues from these durable artifacts rather than requiring the full transcript of previous sessions.

This design allows several agent teams to work concurrently while remaining aware of related work. Humans can inspect the same state, review commits and reports, add comments or tasks, and intervene through the CLI or dashboard. We are already using Horizon for two long-term ungoing projects, Poincaré Conjecture formalization and the Algebraic Jacobian Challenge, where it helps to maintain coherent work across multiple projects, sessions, weeks, and months.

  • Source code and documentation
  • Interactive public demo
  • Blog post

We are also formalizing other important theorems in parallel, such as the bounded gaps between primes theorem. The relevant Lean code can be found at github.com/frenzymath/FormalPantheon

Feedback is very welcome, particularly from anyone working on long-running or multi-project Lean formalizations.

Have you submitted your Algebraic Jacobian Challenge solution to https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval-submissions/? (sorry, I misread the post, see Axel's post below.)
https://lean-lang.org/eval/problems/jacobian_challenge_alggeo/ is still showing no solution.
Did they say they have a solution to Algebraic Jacobian Challenge? The post above just says that they're working on it.

Junyan Xu said :

Have you submitted your Algebraic Jacobian Challenge solution to https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval-submissions/?
https://lean-lang.org/eval/problems/jacobian_challenge_alggeo/ is still showing no solution.

As @Jack McCarthy mentioned, we did not completed the challenge yet. We initially though it would be a smaller-scale project, but we eventually discovered that the challenge requires formalizing significant parts of textbooks (e.g. Mumford "Abelian varieties", Nitsure "Construction of Hilbert and Quot Schemes", Kleiman "The Picard scheme", etc). Therefore, we think it should be seen as a mid-long-term project, and we present it here to argue that Archon Horizon is really helpful to maintain it, and it has already been able to build very useful infrastructure (e.g. Cech Cohomology).

The dashboard of the AJC is publicly available, you can see how Archon Horizon presents on this challenge. While the challenge itself is not solved, I think it shows that Archon Horizon is doing well on the project.
There are several blockers, which seems fair, the mathematics here are difficult, quite modern, and poorly mathlib-supported. Moreover, Fable5/GPT-sol are indeed impressive, but are still making many mistakes and medium lean code quality.
So in projects of this kind, requiring to retrieve/consult several references, trying different proof routes, refactoring existing code, etc, I'd argue that Archon Horizon is much more adapted than bare claude-code/codex, as it is designed to work natively with all of these.

By "the mathematics is quite modern" you mean "the mathematics was all known in the 1960s". This is just an indication of how far away we are from even stating frontier material in some areas of mathematics.

Kevin Buzzard said :

By "the mathematics is quite modern" you mean "the mathematics was all known in the 1960s". This is just an indication of how far away we are from even stating frontier material in some areas of mathematics.

Yes, I agree. We should stay modest toward what AI can do today. The more recent the mathematics, the less training data, hence the more mathematical mistakes.
Therefore, I think the current status of auto-formalization is highly dependent on human supervision, so using Archon Horizon provides tools to supervise. Moreover, since we don't know what are the future outbreaks in AI, using this auto-formalization system can provide better continuity.
